column5: Module 6 callout says the sources do not cover burns, blisters, bites and sprains. Aerie covers them (ch-029 blisters, ch-031 burns, ch-033 sprains, ch-054 stings and bites). Teach a short minor-injuries lesson named for the topic; keep the 'get first-aid training' advice.

Blisters: a hot spot (warm, painful) comes first; prevent with well-fitting broken-in boots laced correctly, wool or synthetic socks not cotton, dry feet, trimmed toenails, tape or blister dressings on hot spots. Small blisters under about 5 mm: protect with a doughnut pad; larger ones may be drained at the lower edge with a sterile needle leaving the skin on, then covered; do not drain in people with diabetes.

Burns: camp stove accidents are one of the most common causes of backcountry burns; set stoves on flat secure ground and wear closed-toe shoes near them. First aid: stop the burning, remove smouldering clothing and jewellery, cool with water (can continue for up to about half an hour for pain; watch for chilling), cover loosely with moist sterile dressings, do not pop blisters. Seek care for blistered burns larger than the casualty's palm (about 1% of body surface), burns to face, hands, feet, genitals or around a limb, any full-thickness burn, or airway signs (singed nose hair, hoarse voice).
Stove placement: 'One of the most common causes of burns in the backcountry is a camp stove accident' (ch-031); flat secure surface and closed-toe footwear. Fits Module 4 lesson 1 stove habits.

Sprains: rest, ice (10 minutes on, 10 off for the first 24 to 48 hours, never directly on skin), compression, elevation, then support. Persistent inability to bear weight, or a sprain that stops someone moving under their own power for more than 24 hours, means getting help out (ch-056).

Hypothermia stages judged in the field by alertness, movement and shivering, not a thermometer: cold stress (shivering, alert, normal movement; not hypothermic) -> mild (shivering hard, clumsy, poor decisions, apathy) -> moderate (shivering weak or stopped, drowsy) -> severe (unresponsive). Most people who feel cold are not hypothermic, but early signs are often ignored. Predisposing: dehydration, exhaustion, alcohol, little food, extremes of age.

Treatment detail: cold stress -> shelter from wind, dry clothes, high-calorie food and drink, then move about. Mild -> handle gently, sit or lie for at least 30 minutes, hypothermia wrap (insulating pad beneath, vapour barrier, sleeping bag including head, windproof outer), warm bottles to the upper trunk wrapped not on bare skin; no food or drink if responsiveness is reduced; get help if no improvement after 30 minutes. Remove wet clothes only if shelter is more than 30 minutes away. Consistent with NHS 'do not rub'.

Trench foot (non-freezing cold injury) from prolonged cold wet feet; symptoms rarely in under 4 days; prevent by drying feet each night and keeping one pair of dry socks for sleeping. Frostnip: white waxy numb skin; rewarm against armpit or a partner's skin. Relevant to multi-day UK wet camping.

CO: colourless, odourless, tasteless; any stove makes it however efficient; never cook in your tent. Extends: haemoglobin binds CO over 200 times more readily than oxygen; a healthy person can take over 4 hours to clear it; rescuers can be overcome in minutes, so protect yourself; suspect CO when several people in a confined space are altered (confirms the Module 6 worked example).

Aerie boil times say 1 minute below 6,000 ft and 3 minutes above 3,000 ft, which is internally inconsistent; the course follows CDC (1 minute; 3 minutes above 6,500 ft). Avoid Aerie's figure. Aerie also says iodine should not be used extensively for more than 2 months; CDC (already cited) says avoid beyond a few weeks; keep the stricter CDC line.

Boiling does not remove farm chemicals or pesticides from run-off; remove debris first. Chemical treatment slows in cold water and is weakened by impurities; halogens are unreliable against Cryptosporidium (confirms CDC). UV is blocked by particles; filter first.

Lightning, absent from the course: count flash to bang; sound travels about 1.6 km every 5 seconds. 30-30 rule: if 30 seconds or less, move to a safer place and stay away from danger for 30 minutes after the last thunder. Descend from summits and ridges; keep away from lone trees and outcrops (at least twice their height), water and open meadows; spread a group 6 to 12 m apart; crouch on an insulating pad, feet together. A building or hard-top vehicle is safest. US statistics not used.

Heat illness, absent from the course: heat exhaustion (tired, nauseous, dizzy, heavy sweating, thirst) -> shade, lie down, cool with water and fanning, sip water with salty food over 1 to 2 hours. Exertional heat stroke: confusion or collapse with very high body temperature (above 40 C) is an emergency: cool the whole body at once (cold water, wet cloths and fanning) and get help. Drinking water alone does not prevent heat illness; pacing and rest matter. Forcing large volumes of plain water can cause low blood sodium.

Stings and anaphylaxis: know group members' allergies and where they keep their adrenaline auto-injector; anaphylaxis = sudden skin signs plus breathing trouble or collapse; help the person use their own auto-injector in the outer mid-thigh; an antihistamine is not a substitute; anyone who needed adrenaline needs emergency care (UK: 999). Mild stings: remove the sting quickly, cold compress.

First aid kit: carry items you know how to use; restock after each trip (confirms REI); contents fit the trip: blister dressings, tape, dressings, gloves, tweezers, scissors, safety pins, a light, pencil and waterproof paper.

Decision making: plan how you would get out before the trip (phone, route out); in an incident STOP and think: scene safe, everyone accounted for, the casualty, then group status, location, weather and resources; then decide stay or go and whether you need help. Scene survey: do not become another casualty (ch-009). Evacuation triggers (ch-056): anaphylaxis, persistent breathlessness or chest pain, any change in consciousness, suspected fracture, cannot bear weight, fever or vomiting beyond 24 hours.
Aerie (US) says monitor a tick bite for up to two weeks and suggests permethrin on clothing; UKHSA says watch for several weeks and names DEET. UK source wins; teach UKHSA.

Aerie recommendations rest on Wilderness Medical Society practice guidelines and are not a substitute for clinical judgment or local protocols; the course should frame its first-aid content as basic awareness and keep pointing to UK training and 999/NHS 111.
